acts.title: A film that travels
text: Every year a few films cross borders that nobody expected them to cross. A Brazilian animated film, released with almost no publicity, wins a prize in France. A Nigerian comedy showcases a city most of its audience will never visit, and then appears on screens in Manchester. Meanwhile some enormous productions, made to appeal to everybody, fail to travel at all.

Distributors used to believe that plot was the thing that travelled, whatever the genre. If a story was simple enough, they argued, audiences anywhere would enjoy following it. That turned out to be only half true. Audiences do tend to prefer a clear plot, but plenty of complicated films have done extremely well abroad, and plenty of simple ones have failed.

What seems to matter more is whether the film lets you recognize something. Stepping on the Flying Grass, set in a village school in Indonesia and based on an original script rather than a novel, is visually stunning and genuinely moving. It is about children who are asked to write about their dreams. One of them wants to help people. One fantasizes about becoming an actress and spends hours practising in front of the mirror. One hopes to eat, just once, in a proper restaurant in the city. You do not need to know anything about Indonesia to know those three children.

The films that fail tend to be the ones that avoid saying anything specific, in case it does not translate. They end up with no particular character, no particular place, and nothing for the audience to hold on to.
Directors who work internationally usually say the same thing: stop trying to be universal. Make something so exact that a stranger can see it.

tts: A beautiful film about the dreams of village school children in rural Indonesia, Stepping on the Flying Grass is both visually stunning and truly moving.
When their teacher asked them to write an essay about their dearest dreams, a group of village schoolchildren began to think seriously about what they planned to do with their lives.
Puji enjoys being useful and just wants to help others.
Mei fantasizes about becoming an actress. She spends hours practising in front of the mirror, but does she really love acting, or is it her mother’s dream?
Agus’s family can’t afford to eat any special food at home, but he really wants to eat at an authentic restaurant in the city.
As the film progresses he gradually realizes that for dreams to come true you need to work at them.

write.q: Write about the kind of films you watch. Use at least two verb + -ing patterns (enjoy, spend time, can’t stand, be worth) and two verb + to + infinitive patterns (hope, tend, want, decide, expect).
write.model: I tend to watch films late at night, usually alone, which probably says something about me. I enjoy watching documentaries most of all — especially the slow ones about people doing an ordinary job extremely well. I spend far too much time reading about films I never actually get round to seeing. What I can’t stand is a predictable thriller: if I have guessed the ending by minute twenty, I stop watching. I hope to see the new animated film from Brazil when it is released here. Everybody says it is worth seeing on a big screen, and I’m looking forward to finding out whether they are right.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute about the last film you saw. Say what you enjoyed, what you can’t stand generally, and whether you would recommend it.
speak.model: The last thing I saw was a documentary about a night bus driver. I enjoy watching that kind of thing — slow, ordinary, one person doing a job properly. I can’t stand predictable thrillers, so it was a relief. It’s worth seeing if you have a quiet evening, and I’d definitely recommend it.
